clue.text: Something should, for a good spell.

definitions.text: Something should, for a good spell.

parts.words: Something should, for a good spell
parts.note: the whole clue describes what a magic spell that is any good ought to do, which is also the idiom for working perfectly

explanation.walkthrough: 'Spell' reads as a stretch of time or of weather, but here it is a magic spell, and a good one should do exactly what the idiom says.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to succeed perfectly, literally what an effective magic charm does.

clue.text: Character proving a little ursine.

parts.note: the whole clue describes a famous storybook figure who is a small bear, ursine meaning bear-like

explanation.walkthrough: Ursine means bear-like. The character is A. A. Milne's teddy bear, 'a bear of very little brain', so he proves a little bear in more than one sense. The answer runs on into 21 down.
explanation.definitionFit: A. A. Milne's storybook teddy is the best-known little bear in children's fiction.

clue.text: Lives with unnatural desires?

indicators.note: unnatural suggests the letters of desires are forced out of their normal order

explanation.surface: A hint at a life lived with perverse cravings.
explanation.definitionFit: To reside somewhere is to live there, so the verbs are synonyms.

clue.text: Get ready to have a child with an old street singer? That's the way to catch somone!

definitions.text: That's the way to catch somone!

parts.words: Get ready to have a child
parts.note: a lying-in was the old term for a mother's confinement before and after giving birth, so to lie in is to prepare for a birth
the waits were bands of street musicians and carol singers in old England, one of them being a wait

explanation.surface: A pregnant woman takes up with a busker, then the clue turns into advice on trapping someone.
explanation.walkthrough: The waits were town musicians who sang and played in the streets, especially at Christmas. The clue's 'somone' is the source's own spelling.
explanation.definitionFit: Hiding and waiting for a person to pass is the classic way to ambush or catch them.

clue.text: A bird may fly better because of its tail.

definitions.text: A bird may fly better because of its tail.

parts.words: A bird may fly better because of its tail
parts.note: the bird of prey shares its name with the paper toy that is steadied in the air by a long tail

explanation.walkthrough: It looks like a remark about birds, but the bird's name is also the toy flown on a string, which really does fly better with a tail.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both a hawk-like bird of prey and the toy flown on a string.

clue.text: When the kids trip over their feet?

definitions.text: When the kids trip over their feet?

parts.words: When the kids trip over their feet
parts.note: the whole clue pictures the clumsy stage of growing up when youngsters stumble about

explanation.walkthrough: 'Trip' could be an outing, but here it is literal stumbling, which is what the gawky early-teen years bring.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names the gangly, self-conscious stage of adolescence when young people are clumsy.

clue.text: Any he-animal gets shook up, but one just laughs.

indicators.note: shook up means jumbled, so the letters of 'any he' are shaken into a new order

explanation.surface: A male animal gets rattled while another merely laughs it off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gets shook up' rearranges the letters of ANY HE; 'animal' belongs to the surface, telling you a beast is coming. 'One just laughs' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The spotted hyena is famous for a call that sounds like human laughter.

clue.text: Sounds like the rule for pouring.

indicators.note: sounds like tells you to say a word aloud and enter one that is pronounced the same

parts.note: a monarch's rule is their reigning

explanation.surface: Someone states a rule for how to pour a drink.
explanation.definitionFit: When it is pouring, rain is falling heavily, so the two words describe the same weather.

clue.text: Evidently I'm accompanied by 21 down, if you'll just be patient!

parts.note: 21 down finishes the storybook character, who is a bear
to be accompanied by someone is to be with them
I am, seen from outside, is me

explanation.surface: Someone asks for patience while saying they come with a companion from elsewhere in the grid.
explanation.walkthrough: The 21 down character is a bear, so 'I'm accompanied by' him is put in the order of the familiar plea for patience; 'Evidently' points out that the clue spells it out literally.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a polite request to be patient while the speaker carries on.

clue.text: Just now appearing in China's centennial…

indicators.note: in tells you the answer sits inside the words China's centennial, across the word break

parts.note: the answer runs unbroken through the end of China's and the start of centennial

explanation.surface: Something newly emerging during China's hundredth-anniversary celebrations.
explanation.definitionFit: Nascent describes something just coming into being, which is a close synonym of newly emerging.

clue.text: …and an Egyptian title given over a century ago.

definitions.text: …and an Egyptian title given over a century ago.

parts.words: and an Egyptian title given over a century ago
parts.note: the whole clue describes the title the Ottoman sultan granted to the ruler of Egypt in 1867

explanation.walkthrough: The dots tie it to the previous clue's centennial. In 1867 the Ottoman sultan granted Egypt's viceroy this Persian-derived title, a little over a century before this 1975 puzzle.
explanation.definitionFit: The khedives were the viceroys who ruled Egypt for the Ottomans from 1867 until 1914.

clue.text: One might in starting the story of how a minor collision may end.

definitions.text: One might in starting the story
definitions.meaning: first meaning: a writer may set the opening line of a story in from the margin

definitions.text: how a minor collision may end
definitions.meaning: second meaning, read as two words

explanation.walkthrough: The second half splits the answer into IN DENT: a fender-bender ends in a dent. The first half uses the verb for setting a line in from the margin.
explanation.definitionFit: To indent is to begin a line further from the margin, as at the start of a paragraph.

clue.text: A valeric change in the manner of such as Charles.

definitions.text: in the manner of such as Charles

indicators.note: change says the letters of 'a valeric' are altered into another order

explanation.surface: A chemistry note about valeric acid altering, next to a remark about a king's style.
explanation.walkthrough: Valeric is a real chemistry word, which hides that 'change' acts on A VALERIC as fodder. Charles is King Charles I, whose Royalist supporters in the English Civil War were known as Cavaliers.
explanation.definitionFit: Charles I's followers were Cavaliers, and the adjective describes their dashing, offhand style.

clue.text: It might be the express law golfers break.

indicators.note: golfers breaking the law suggests the letters of 'law golfers' being broken apart and rebuilt

explanation.surface: Golfers breaking a law about speed, as though on an express train.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface invites thoughts of speed limits, but 'break' signals an anagram of LAW GOLFERS. Wells Fargo ran the famous stagecoach express service in the American West.
explanation.definitionFit: Wells Fargo & Company was a famous American express carrier of mail and valuables by stagecoach.

clue.text: Alga, possibly.

parts.note: an alga may be an example of marine plant growth such as kelp or wrack

explanation.walkthrough: Plain as it looks, the 'possibly' marks the answer as one kind of alga rather than a synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: Kelp, wrack and other marine algae are all commonly called by this general name.

clue.text: War might be — on a salary?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a war is said to be ..., that is carried on
second meaning: someone on a salary is in paid work

explanation.walkthrough: The two halves use the same spelling as a past participle of 'wage war' and as an adjective meaning paid.
explanation.definitionFit: One meaning is carried on, as a campaign; the other means earning regular pay.

clue.text: Possibly a more wise description might be tedious.

indicators.note: possibly suggests 'a more wise' might be rearranged into something else

explanation.surface: A wiser account of something could turn out dull.
explanation.definitionFit: Something wearisome tires you out with boredom, so it is a synonym of tedious.

clue.text: It certainly doesn't mean you've got it all together, making up lips as red as this.

definitions.text: It certainly doesn't mean you've got it all together

indicators.note: making up means composing, so the letters of 'lips as red' are made up into a new word

explanation.surface: A lipstick tip: making your lips this red doesn't mean you have your life in order.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Making up' looks like applying makeup to the lips, but it signals the anagram of LIPS AS RED.
explanation.definitionFit: Dispersal is the scattering of things apart, the opposite of everything being gathered together.

clue.text: I objectively returned, and came across the less familiar name of a social worker.

definitions.text: the less familiar name of a social worker

indicators.note: returned means the word for I in the objective case is sent back the other way

parts.note: I used as an object, rather than a subject, is me
to come across someone is to have met them

explanation.surface: Someone back from somewhere meets a social worker under an unusual name.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Returned' turns ME into EM. The social worker is an ant, since ants live in organised colonies, and emmet is an old dialect word for one.
explanation.definitionFit: Emmet is an archaic and dialect name for an ant, an insect famous for its social colonies.

clue.text: The cutter came the wrong way, evidently.

indicators.note: coming the wrong way suggests the letters of 'came the' arrive in a jumbled order

explanation.surface: A ship or a blade appears from the wrong direction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cutter' suggests a boat that could come the wrong way, but it is a blade.
explanation.definitionFit: A machete is a broad, heavy knife used for cutting through vegetation.

clue.text: Carry a challenge in your suitcase, perhaps?

parts.note: to lug something is to carry it with effort
a gage is a pledge thrown down as a challenge to fight, like a glove

explanation.surface: Packing a dare in your case for a trip.
explanation.walkthrough: A gage is an old word for a glove or token thrown down as a challenge.
explanation.definitionFit: A suitcase is one example of the bags and cases travellers take with them.

clue.text: This remarkable animal can hide in disguise.

indicators.note: in disguise means the letters of 'can hide' appear in altered form

explanation.surface: An unusual creature that can camouflage itself.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hide' looks like the animal's trick, but 'in disguise' rearranges the letters of CAN HIDE. The echidna, or spiny anteater, is remarkable as one of the few egg-laying mammals.
explanation.definitionFit: The echidna is an Australian spiny anteater, unusual as a mammal that lays eggs.

clue.text: Measured by the feet, obviously.

parts.note: the whole clue describes measuring a distance by counting one's steps

explanation.walkthrough: 'Feet' looks like the unit of length, but here it means the walker's own feet, used to step out a distance.
explanation.definitionFit: To pace something off is to measure a distance by walking it and counting strides.

clue.text: See 1 down
A long drawn-out speech.

parts.note: drawn-out suggests a lengthy address but literally means the vowels are stretched in speaking

explanation.walkthrough: It reads like a tedious oration, but the speech is a manner of speaking with slow, stretched vowels.
explanation.definitionFit: A drawl is a slow way of speaking in which vowel sounds are lengthened.

clue.text: See 8 down
Short statement in passing?

parts.note: passing is a euphemism for dying, and the statement is the newspaper notice of a death, here in clipped form

explanation.walkthrough: 'In passing' suggests a casual aside, but passing here means death; the answer is the short form of obituary.
explanation.definitionFit: An obituary is a published notice of someone's death; the short form is a common abbreviation.

clue.text: Start the tune with something fresh (we hope).

parts.note: to open something is to start it
an air is a tune or melody

explanation.surface: A musician begins a piece with something new.
explanation.walkthrough: The bracketed 'we hope' admits that outdoor air is not always fresh.
explanation.definitionFit: The outdoors is where fresh air is found, at least in principle.

clue.text: What none but the brave deserve?

definitions.text: What none but the brave deserve?

parts.words: What none but the brave deserve
parts.note: Dryden's line says none but the brave deserves the fair, and fair-haired people are fair

explanation.walkthrough: The line is from Dryden's poem 'Alexander's Feast': 'None but the brave deserves the fair.' Fair there means beautiful women, but read as fair-haired it gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Fair hair is light yellow, so the fair can be read as people with golden hair.

clue.text: Sounds as though someone brought a ringer to the dance?

definitions.text: Sounds as though someone brought a ringer to the dance?

parts.words: Sounds as though someone brought a ringer to the dance
parts.note: the phrase for the most admired woman at a dance is pronounced like a bell, a thing that rings, at the ball

explanation.walkthrough: A ringer suggests a substitute or impostor, but here it is simply a bell; said aloud, 'bell of the ball' gives the phrase for the star of the dance.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names the most admired and attractive woman at a dance or party.
